title: Problem 1.1
statement_text: Determine the smallest $m$ such that in every $2$-coloring of the edges of the ordered complete graph $K_{m}$, there is a monochromatic non-nested matching of size $n$.
context_text: This is a problem from the open problem session of the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025), presented by János Barát. The vertices of the complete graph $K_m$ are identified with $\{1,\dots,m\}$ in this order. Two independent edges $ij$ and $st$ (with $i<j$, $s<t$) are nested if $i<s<t<j$ or $s<i<j<t$; a non-nested matching is a matching in which no two edges are nested. In the unordered setting, $3n-1$ vertices always force a monochromatic matching with $n$ edges, and this is tight. Here the answer is trivially between $3n-1$ and $4n-2$, and Barát, Gyárfás and Tóth conjectured that the lower bound $3n-1$ is optimal. The upper bound was improved by a small additive constant (with small cases checked up to $n=5$ or $6$), and a more substantial improvement relies on a Turán-type conjecture that Barát, Freschi and Tóth can prove only with a small error term: once this error term is erased, $m>(2+\sqrt3)n$ would suffice.

title: Problem 2.1
statement_text: Let $G$ be a random 4-regular graph. Is it true that the coefficient of $P_{G}$ at $\prod_{v\in V(G)}v^{2}$ is a.a.s. non-zero?
context_text: Problem presented by Zdeněk Dvořák at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A random 4-regular graph is here the union of two independent uniformly random Hamiltonian cycles on the same vertex set (a multigraph, simple with constant probability; a uniformly random 4-regular graph a.a.s. contains two disjoint Hamiltonian cycles, and the union of four random perfect matchings is another a.a.s. equivalent model); a.a.s. means with probability tending to $1$. Such a graph is a.a.s. 3-colourable, but it is open whether it is a.a.s. 3-choosable. The graph polynomial is $P_G=\prod_{uv\in E(G)}(u-v)$, whose variables correspond to the vertices of $G$. By the Alon–Tarsi theorem, if the coefficient of $\prod_{v}v^{f(v)}$ in $P_G$ is non-zero for some $f:V(G)\to\{0,\dots,k-1\}$, then $G$ is $k$-choosable. All monomials of $P_G$ have total degree $|E(G)|$, so for a 4-regular graph the only relevant monomial with exponents at most $2$ is $\prod_v v^2$, and a positive answer would show that random 4-regular graphs are a.a.s. 3-choosable. In the two Hamiltonian cycles model the expected value of the coefficient is zero, so a proof would need an anti-concentration inequality, and a disproof a concentration result.

title: Problem 3.1
statement_text: Let $G$ be a disjoint union of cycles. Let $H$ be a disjoint union of $K_{4}$'s. Is $G\cup H$ 4-colourable?
context_text: Problem presented by Penny Haxell at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). Here $G$ and $H$ are graphs on the same vertex set, so the components of $H$ (copies of $K_4$) partition the vertices; asking whether $G\cup H$ is 4-colourable for all such $H$ amounts to asking whether a graph of maximum degree $2$ is strongly $4$-colourable, i.e. for every partition of its vertices into sets of size $4$ it has a proper colouring in which each set receives four distinct colours. If $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_5$'s, then $G\cup H$ is 5-colourable; if $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_3$'s, $G\cup H$ need not be 3-colourable. This is a special case of a general question on the strong chromatic number: if $G$ has maximum degree $d$ and $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_{2d}$'s, is $G\cup H$ $(2d)$-colourable? The value $2d$ would be best possible, and Haxell proved that $G\cup H$ is $(3d-1)$-colourable when $H$ is a disjoint union of $K_{3d-1}$'s.

title: Problem 4.1
statement_text:
Is it true that every diamond-free claw-free cubic graph is strongly 6-edge-colorable?
In other words, is it true that $\chi^{\prime}_{s}(T(G))=6$ for every cubic graph $G$?
context_text: Problem presented by František Kardoš at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A strong edge colouring assigns colours to the edges so that any two edges that are adjacent or joined by an edge receive distinct colours (i.e. a proper colouring of the square of the line graph); the strong chromatic index $\chi'_s(G)$ is the minimum number of colours. A graph is claw-free if it has no induced $K_{1,3}$, and diamond-free if it has no diamond ($K_4$ minus an edge) as a subgraph. The truncation $T(G)$ of a cubic graph $G$ is the cubic graph obtained by replacing each vertex by a triangle; it is well known that the diamond-free claw-free cubic graphs are exactly the truncations of cubic graphs, which explains the equivalence of the two formulations. Lv, Li and Zhang proved that every claw-free subcubic graph other than the triangular prism has $\chi'_s(G)\le8$; Lin and Lin improved this to $7$, with an infinite family of tight examples, all of which contain diamonds. Han and Cui proved that truncated prisms are strongly 6-edge-colourable.

title: Problem 5.1
statement_text:
If a cubic graph admits a $2$-homogeneous coloring,
then $4$ colors are always sufficient.
context_text: Problem presented by Borut Lužar and Roman Soták at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A $k$-homogeneous colouring is a proper vertex colouring in which exactly $k$ colours appear in the open neighbourhood of every vertex. A graph has a $1$-homogeneous colouring if and only if it is bipartite. Not every cubic graph has a $2$-homogeneous colouring: for example, a cubic graph containing as a subgraph a triangular prism with one edge of a triangle subdivided does not. Bipartite cubic graphs admit a $2$-homogeneous colouring with at most $6$ colours (Janicová, Madaras, Soták and Lužar), and the problem asks for the minimum number of colours that suffices for every cubic graph admitting a $2$-homogeneous colouring; a weaker version, for bipartite cubic graphs only, appeared in the earlier paper. The statement is proposed as a conjecture based on preliminary research.
notes: Stated as a declarative conjecture inside a labeled Problem environment; a weaker bipartite version appeared in prior work [2].
paper_title: Open problems of the 33rd Workshop on Cycles and Colourings

title: Problem 5.2
statement_text: There is a finite number of connected bridgeless cubic graphs that do not admit a $2$-homogeneous coloring.
context_text: Problem presented by Borut Lužar and Roman Soták at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). A $k$-homogeneous colouring is a proper vertex colouring in which exactly $k$ colours appear in the open neighbourhood of every vertex. A graph has a $1$-homogeneous colouring if and only if it is bipartite. Not every cubic graph has a $2$-homogeneous colouring: for example, a cubic graph containing as a subgraph a triangular prism with one edge of a triangle subdivided does not. The proposers ask which cubic graphs admit a $2$-homogeneous colouring and, based on preliminary research, conjecture that only finitely many connected bridgeless cubic graphs fail to admit one (they also conjecture that $4$ colours always suffice when one exists).
notes: Stated as a declarative conjecture inside a labeled Problem environment.

title: Conjecture 6.1
statement_text: Each bridgeless graph admits a $2$-flow $\varphi_{2}$ and a $4$-flow $\varphi_{4}$ such that for any edge $e$, if $\varphi_{2}(e)=0$, then $|\varphi_{4}(e)|\geq 2$.
context_text: Conjecture presented by Jozef Rajník at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025). For an integer $k\ge2$, a $k$-flow of a graph is an orientation of the edges with integer values $\varphi(e)$, $|\varphi(e)|<k$ (zero allowed), such that at every vertex the incoming and outgoing sums are equal; a circular $r$-flow is a real-valued flow with $1\le|f(e)|\le r-1$ on every edge. The conjecture implies Tutte's 5-flow conjecture, since $(5\varphi_2+\varphi_4)/2$ is then a circular $5$-flow. It generalises Seymour's approach in the proof of the 6-flow theorem, where a pair of a 2-flow and a 3-flow played a crucial role: besides forbidding the pair of values $(0,0)$ on an edge, the conjecture also forbids $(0,\pm1)$. Such a pair is called a $1/2$-flow-pair. It has been verified for all cyclically 4-edge-connected snarks up to $34$ vertices, all snarks with circular flow number $5$ on $36$ vertices, and snarks of oddness $4$ up to $44$ vertices.

title: Problem 7.1
statement_text: Every bicritical snark is almost-$\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{2}$-connected and almost-$\mathbb{Z}_{4}$-connected.
context_text: Problem presented by Nikolay Ulyanov at the 33rd Cycles and Colourings workshop (2025), following the terminology of Jaeger, Linial, Payan and Tarsi. Let $G$ be a directed graph and $A$ a non-trivial abelian group; the boundary of $f:E\to A$ is $\partial f(x)=\sum_{e\text{ leaving }x}f(e)-\sum_{e\text{ entering }x}f(e)$. A map $b:V\to A$ with $\sum_x b(x)=0$ is admissible if $b=\partial f$ for some $f:E\to A\setminus\{0\}$, and $G$ is $A$-connected if every such $b$ is admissible; $G$ is almost-$A$-connected if every such $b$ is admissible except $b=0$ (i.e. $G$ has no nowhere-zero $A$-flow, but all other boundaries are admissible). Here a snark is a cubic, non-3-edge-colourable, cyclically 4-edge-connected graph of girth at least $5$; it is bicritical if removing any two distinct vertices yields a 3-edge-colourable graph, and critical if this holds for any two adjacent vertices. Non-3-edge-colourable cubic graphs have neither a nowhere-zero $\mathbb{Z}_4$-flow nor a nowhere-zero $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$-flow. By exhaustive search, the Petersen graph and both Blanuša snarks on $18$ vertices are almost-$\mathbb{Z}_2^2$- and almost-$\mathbb{Z}_4$-connected, whereas Tietze's graph, all snarks on $24$ vertices (all non-bicritical) and the smallest critical non-bicritical snarks on $32$ vertices are not. The problem emerged from exploring the House of Graphs snark database.
notes: Stated as a declarative conjecture inside a labeled Problem environment.
